## Winners and Losers of Desert Green Energy

Chianese, Robert Louis . Chianese, Robert Louis.

ProQuest document link

## ABSTRACT (ENGLISH)

The four majestic deserts in the American Southwest extend for 137,700,000 hectares. To casual visitors, these deserts might look like blank spaces or forbidding wastelands. Yet they support thousands of species of plants and hundreds of bird, reptile, mammal, and insect species, all living in tense interdependence. Then humans entered the picture, upsetting the delicate balance. Increasingly, people are using the desert floor to install vast fields of solar power systems to combat global warming. These systems produce electricity without greenhouse gas emissions and reduce the need for fossil fuel power plants, along with the associated infrastructure. But they come with environmental disruptions of their own. Solar power systems disturb the habitats of burrowing owls, desert foxes, and many others, reducing their numbers. Conversely, populations of ravens (Corvus corax) are soaring to unprecedented and disruptive levels.

## FULL TEXT

## Headnote

Solar installations and urban sprawl in the Mojave have helped raven numbers soar at the cost of vulnerable prey. The four majestic deserts in the American Southwest extend for 137,700,000 hectares. To casual visitors, these deserts might look like blank spaces or forbidding wastelands. Yet they support thousands of species of plants and hundreds of bird, reptile, mammal, and insect species, all living in tense interdependence. Then humans entered the picture, upsetting the delicate balance.

Increasingly, we are using the desert floor to install vast fields of solar power systems to combat global warming. These systems produce electricity without greenhouse gas emissions and reduce the need for fossil fuel power plants, along with the associated infrastructure. But they come with environmental disruptions of their own. Solar power systems disturb the habitats of burrowing owls, desert foxes, and many others, reducing their numbers. Conversely, populations of ravens (Corvus corax) are soaring to unprecedented and disruptive levels.

In the Mojave Desert, which is located primarily in California and Nevada, towers supporting the transmission lines that carry green energy provide ravens with convenient nesting areas and unnaturally high perches. From this convenient new vantage point, ravens can scour the desert floor for a vulnerable prey: the desert tortoise (Gopherus agassizii). Desert tortoises can live to 50 years of age, but they must turn four before their shells are hard enough to protect them from a raven's hooked and pointed beak. Today, at the base of many towers, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service conservationists regularly find a midden of juvenile tortoise shells that have been pierced on top for the kill and then scooped out inside for the tasty meal.

Surrounding development has intensified this shifting dynamic between predator and prey. People want to keep building their homes, resorts, casinos, restaurants, and golf courses. To do so, they need more power. And they imagine that green energy can bail them out with no environmental cost. But green solutions come with costs of their own. In addition, the water features, greenery, and garbage that accompany human development now provide steady sustenance and shade for ravens, so that these once migratory birds stay in place year-round. As a result, the raven population in the Mojave has increased sharply, with huge flocks of hundreds of birds (prejudicially referred to as "conspiracies of ravens") regularly blanketing the sky. Biologist Bill Boarman estimates that raven populations in the Mojave have increased 1,000 percent since the 1960s, as noted in the April 2023 issue of Smithsonian Magazine. Meanwhile, the population of the desert tortoise-which is endemic, or geographically specific, to the Mojave-has

shrunk to less than 10 percent of its historic numbers, mainly due to raven predation. Since 1990, the species has been listed as threatened by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.

This unintended consequence of our quest for green energy, combined with ongoing development and evergrowing energy use, illustrates a difficult ecological reality: Human solutions for environmental concerns often come with disruptive trade-offs that force new adjustments to rebalance the system. In other words, one eco-fix can cause new eco-harms.

Through wildlife population management strategies, citizen science initiatives, and technofixes, researchers are trying to boost desert tortoise numbers and keep ravens in check. But that effort raises yet another troubling question of trade-offs. In the quest to right our environmental disturbances, how far are we willing to go toward suppressing-or even culling-one native species to save another?

Development Versus Biodiversity

The tale of the desert tortoise's demise began well before the first raven discovered a transmission line tower transporting green energy. Since 1982, when the energy firm Solar One installed the first solar power plant in the Mojave, power companies have steadily destroyed the desert tortoise's home by clearing and leveling the desert surface to accommodate ever more green energy installations, including solar panels, curved trough systems, mirror concentrated systems, and wind installations. (See "Rearranging the Planet to Save It," January-February 2018.) In 2010, nine solar projects received 16,000 hectares of desert from the Bureau of Land Management. These developments were in the western Mojave, where the best solar energy sites coincide with prime desert tortoise habitat. Understanding this threat, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service has actively translocated tortoises from regions zoned for green power installation to sites with perimeter fencing that can control their population density and disease transmission.

Meanwhile, conservationists have also moved tortoises from land destined for other human uses, such as housing, commercial development, and military bases. But relocating desert tortcises causes half of them to urinate their summer-long water supply and die. Only 25 percent of those moved survive.

Non-native invasive grasses such as cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum) and Arabian grass (Schismus barbatus) further threaten desert tortoise survival by presenting a non-nutritive food source and a vegetative cover that easily catches the desert on fire. The tortoises that manage to withstand these landscape threats still must survive the ravens. Some conservationists are working to help tortoises achieve their best defense against ravens: age. With additional years comes a hardened shell that helps tortoises resist raven assaults from above. In 2014, conservation biologist Kristin Berry of the U.S. Geological Survey and colleagues reported in Herpetological Monographs that the Desert Tortoise Research Natural Area, which is surrounded by fencing and forbids livestock and vehicles, had greater tortoise numbers and a lower tortoise death rate than surrounding regions.

Artificial burrows can safeguard young tortoises from ravens until they are old enough and tough enough to be reintroduced to the open desert. But this intervention has to be conducted carefully because captive-bred animals have a 50 percent mortality rate. In 2024, the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance reported success in reintroducing 70 young tortoises into the wild. How these tortoises will fare as they slowly mature will be of great interest to all desert and tortoise lovers.

## Pressing the Predators

Meanwhile, conservationists have long aimed to lift tortoise populations up by pushing raven numbers down. There are no easy fixes, and some population management methods can seem gruesome at first blush. They have taught ravens to eat chicken eggs, which they then replaced with poisoned ones. They have also located and destroyed raven nests in the high towers, or sprayed raven eggs with oil, which kills the embryos by depriving them of oxygen. This approach keeps raven parents on the nest, which prevents the laying of a second batch.

In 2008, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service produced a lengthy study of methods to reduce raven depredation of Mojave tortoises. In an updated version published in 2023, the authors examined nonlethal deterrents, such as removing new food sources-a major contributing factor to the raven population explosion. But that strategy did not meet the goal of a 75 percent reduction in raven numbers, nor did moving raven nests. Effigies in the form of raven

carcasses hung upside down did scare the birds off, but that approach is likely too grotesque to be used in in- habited areas. Trapping ravens has also worked, but not with large groups.

The Living Desert Zoo and Gardens in Palm Desert, California, once implemented a low-tech program to cut off the ravens' access to garbage bins that provide an abundant food supply in the fast-growing towns through the Mojave. Volunteers walked restaurant areas checking on whether the bins were securely covered. Finding covered bins five times in a row merited a gold star, which restaurants could display as a sign of being a good ecological neighbor. In 2020, 17 restaurants in the city of Twentynine Palms, California, earned the award-close to 40 percent of the restaurants in the city.

Technofixes for Raven Troubles

High-tech strategies may one day provide more effective forms of deterrence. Such tactics may include putting GPS tracking monitors on ravens and using drones to locate and scare the birds. Drones have even been used to spray raven eggs with oil.

One effective deterrent is green light from lasers. The laser beam doesn't harm the ravens, but it does drive them away. Some municipalities have installed lasers at landfills. Tim Shields, a biologist and inventor, points green laser light at ravens in favored gathering spots to make them wary of returning. This strategy, however, involves human spotters and shooters, which is hardly cost effective.

To address this problem, Shields has worked on devising a new delivery system. As founder of the former Hardshell Labs, and now as president of the Nevada-based OrniLogic, Shields is seeking new solutions to complex environmental problems, often through developing novel technologies. Shields has built a prototype of a small robotic desert rover with a camera and green laser beam device that can be controlled remotely by a cell phone or computer.

Shields has also designed even more elaborate forms of aversion therapy. Since 2014, his team has been perfecting 3D-printed versions of baby tortoises, which they call Techno-Torts. He arms these look-alikes with a buried explosive device that shoots grape Kool-Aid up through the shell and onto any raven that attempts a nibble. The raven pierces the shell, gets doused and frightened, and then becomes averse to actual tortoise shells. The idea is that, after encountering the Techno-Tort, ravens' social communicative nature will lead the birds to teach their young and other members of the flock to stop preying on tortoises.

In my October 2025 discussions with Shields, he claimed highly effective results at the individual raven level. But he noted that the strategy is less effective for larger groups of birds. For dense flocks, the green laser beams seem to work well. According to Shields, only 1 percent of ravens return to the laser shooting area, and less than 1 percent become insensitive to the green light. But human beings have to operate the lasers with conscious control through the videostreamed cameras and firing mechanisms, and there are legal concerns about using lasers. Ethical Dilemma with No Solution?

Even as environmentalists try with limited success to keep the raven population in check, the energy demands that originally drove up the population continue to grow, along with the climate crisis that made us turn toward green energy in the first place.

An obvious first step is to encourage people to use less electricity. But after four decades of conservation measures, the commercial, industrial, and residential sectors use more electricity now than in 1990.

Current forecasts suggest that 2025 and 2026 will exceed the all-time high for U.S. electricity consumption set in 2024, with a projected average annual growth rate of about 1.7 percent between 2020 and 2026. We must acknowledge that an effective, economical strategy to keep and expand our green energy systems while saving the desert tortoise-and the many other species threatened by our desert encroachment-may be hard to find.

One remaining solution for the desert tortoise, killing adult ravens, is unsavory to many. The species is protected in the United States by the Migratory Bird Treaty Act of 1918. Ravens are also sacred to Native Americans and they are respected by many environmentalists.

Should we rethink our approach to this dilemma? Environmental ethics about killing invasive species involve complex principles. For example, the eradication should not involve unnecessary suffering. And the impacts on the

environment and other native species must not be severe. Ravens, although a protected native species, are out of control. Because of their predatory behaviors, conservation biologists are now labeling them as an "invasive native." Does that label make ravens fairer game for culling? Should they be removed from protection? We seem to accept lethal pest control of gophers, ground squirrels, skunks, and raccoons when they invade our living spaces. And deer hunting is permitted in many states and municipalities for the sake of forest vegetation and the health of the deer's own population. Should we start thinking about ravens in a similar way?

Even if we chose to kill the raven, a native bird, in order to protect another native animal, the strategy might not work. A 1990 draft environmental impact statement by the Bureau of Land Management noted that using shooting as the only tactic to control ravens is impractical because the birds readily learn to avoid human shooters and the shots can damage transmission towers. Chemical castration of ravens might prove effective, suggests master falconer Steve Shaw of the Prairie Falcon Conservancy in Templeton, California. This technique has been used experimentally in rats. But the effects wear off without further dosing, which creates an open-ended expense.

We are left today with several unsatisfactory options for fixing the ecoharm we created when we planted our green power systems on the living desert floor and allowed homes and businesses to expand into sensitive desert ecosystems. We could continue our existing raven control measures, but they don't seem to be working quickly enough to save the desert tortoise. We could conduct more research in the hopes of identifying more effective controls. We could even begin selective culling of the raven flocks through shooting, as ineffective and controversial as that might be.

If we do not discover an acceptable and effective solution soon, we may have to leave the ravens on their flight path to even higher numbers, overwhelming the ground-hugging desert tortoises. Each of us must consider how committed we are to fixing this imbalance we caused in the Mojave. What might it require from us to remedy the disturbance we created? And might whatever solution we land on once again invoke that bothersome eco-paradox: Will a new eco-fix produce a new eco-harm?

## QUICK TAKE

Transmission line towers channeling green energy across the Mojave Desert offer ravens new perches for spotting their prey: the desert tortoise.

Past remediation efforts to slow raven population growth, such as scaring off colonies and destroying eggs, have had limited success.

Humans gave ravens an advantage, but it's unclear how far we are willing to go to suppress this native bird species and bring the desert tortoise back from the brink.

The population of the desert tortoise has shrunk to less than 10 percent of its historic numbers, mainly due to raven predation.
